item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports history interventions as probes of recommendation behavior. [Measuring Recency Bias (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) introduces a recency-bias metric and reports that reducing excessive recency emphasis improves accuracy across evaluated models. [FCESR (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.13632) distinguishes sufficiency—whether retaining a small history subset preserves a recommendation—from necessity—whether removing it changes the recommendation. [Demystifying Sequential Recommendations (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.03606) searches for minimal discrete history edits using genetic algorithms, reporting high model fidelity across three datasets and three models. A [2026 Shapley-based framework](https://jidmis.org/index.php/jidmis/article/view/2525) evaluates temporal attribution through removal faithfulness, robustness, sufficiency, and mask-versus-shuffle consistency.\n\nSuggested diagnostic synthesis: compare removal of recent repeated-interest evidence, removal of isolated interactions, and order shuffling against matched random perturbations. Define repeated interests using observable item recurrence or title/description similarity; treat these as behavioral proxies. Match deletion counts and, where feasible, recency and popularity; separate content removal from position changes by comparing deletion/repacking with masking. Shuffle older history while holding the last item fixed, then shuffle the full history to distinguish broader order sensitivity from last-item dependence. Measure original recommendation rank changes, score margins, and top-10 overlap using fixed candidates and unchanged eligibility filters. Add retention-only probes for sufficiency. Report paired differences against random controls and variation across users/categories. These interventions reveal model dependence on observed history; they do not establish actual user intent or real-world causal preference effects."}
